38126: Your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit, so you should not smoke, overeat or neglect exercise. 1 Corinthians 3:16-17 and 6:19 are taken together as teaching about looking after one's individual body.

Wright stress that for a Jew the temple was the one place where God's presence dwelt among his people, so calling a Gentile house church God's temple is breathtaking. 1 Cor 6:19 does apply to individual bodies, but the issue there is sex with prostitutes, not diet: your body is joined to Christ and must not be joined to a prostitute.
38128: Evangelical scholars generally agree with this exegesis; Fee is himself a Pentecostal evangelical. They add that 6:19-20 really does teach that the individual body belongs to God and should be used to glorify him (1 Cor 6:20), so a careful application to stewardship of health is not wrong, provided it does not replace the main point. This is mostly a popular misunderstanding, not a scholarly dispute.
38129: Reading 3:16 as about the community means church division is a sacrilege, a far stronger warning than most readers hear. It also keeps the sexual ethics of 6:19 from being reduced to general wellness.
38130: 1 Corinthians 13 as a wedding reading about romantic love

38132: Chapter 13 sits between two chapters about spiritual gifts in worship. Paul is telling a competitive church that tongues, prophecy and knowledge without love are worthless. Scholars across traditions, such as Anthony Thiselton and David Garland, agree.

Evangelical pastors note that the love described is the love Christ shows and applies to every relationship, marriage included, so reading it at a wedding is fine if the couple hears it as a costly, cross-shaped commitment rather than a feeling.
38134: Heard in context, the chapter is a sharp challenge to churches that prize gifted performers over humble love.
38135: Women silent in church (1 Cor 14:34-35) as a simple universal rule

38138: Complementarian scholars such as D. A. Carson and Wayne Grudem argue that the verses are original (they are in all manuscripts, only placed differently) and that Paul restricts women from the authoritative weighing of prophecy, a role tied to church leadership, rather than all speech. Egalitarian and complementarian scholars both reject the idea that women may never speak. The wider debate belongs to /debates/gender-roles.
38139: How this text is read shapes women's participation in worship worldwide; seeing that 1 Cor 11:5 already assumes women speak narrows the real question.
38140: A young church learned that being 'spiritual' meant serving the weak, that sexual and religious choices mattered because bodies belong to the Lord, and that the resurrection of the body was the heart of their hope.
38141: Churches today face the same temptations: celebrity leaders, class divisions at the table, gifts used for show, freedom that ignores the conscience of others, and a vague spirituality without bodily resurrection. 1 Corinthians answers each one with the cross and the resurrection.
38142: Paul, hurt and accused of being weak, defends his ministry by showing that the gospel's power always comes through weakness, suffering and generous self-giving, just as it did in Christ.
38144: Paul, the church's founder, now in a damaged relationship with it; Timothy had been his envoy to Corinth (1 Cor 4:17).

38148: The church in Corinth and believers throughout Achaia

Titus brought news that most of the church had repented (2 Cor 7:6-13). But newcomers, whom Paul sarcastically calls 'super-apostles' (2 Cor 11:5), had arrived with letters of recommendation, impressive speaking and Jewish credentials, and they mocked Paul as weak in person and unprofessional for refusing pay.
38150: Paul's 'painful visit' to Corinth and the 'tearful letter' (dates approximate).
38151: Riot of the silversmiths in Ephesus (Acts 19:23-41); Paul may refer to deadly danger in Asia around this time (2 Cor 1:8-10).
38152: Paul writes 2 Corinthians from Macedonia while gathering the collection.
38153: Paul spends three months in Greece, presumably Corinth, and writes Romans (Acts 20:2-3), suggesting the reconciliation largely succeeded.
38154:
2 Corinthians comes out of a broken relationship. After 1 Corinthians, things got worse. Paul made a quick, painful visit; someone in the church wronged him publicly (2 Cor 2:5-8, 2 Cor 7:12); and he wrote a severe letter 'with many tears' that is probably lost. He changed his travel plans to avoid another painful visit and was then accused of being fickle (2 Cor 1:15-23). He nearly died in Asia, despairing even of life (2 Cor 1:8-9). When Titus finally met him in Macedonia with good news, Paul wrote with relief.

The letter's tone shifts sharply. Chapters 1-9 are warm and reconciling; chapters 10-13 are biting, ironic and defensive. Many scholars, including Margaret Thrall and Victor Furnish, think chapters 10-13 were a separate letter, possibly the tearful letter itself or a later one written after fresh bad news. Others, such as Murray Harris, David Garland and Ben Witherington, defend the letter's unity, explaining the shift as Paul turning from the repentant majority to the remaining opponents. Chapters 8 and 9 both address the collection and may also have been separate notes. The question does not change the letter's message, but it helps explain why it reads unevenly.

The rival teachers were Jewish believers ('Are they Hebrews? So am I', 2 Cor 11:22) who offered what Corinth admired: polished rhetoric, visions, letters of recommendation and a ministry that charged fees like a respectable teacher. Unlike the opponents in Galatia, they do not seem to have pushed circumcision. Paul's response is to boast, but to boast like a fool, listing beatings, shipwrecks, hunger and anxiety, and finally a humiliating escape over the wall of Damascus, the opposite of the Roman honour of being first over an enemy wall.
38155: Travelling teachers carried letters from patrons vouching for them. Paul says the Corinthian church is his letter, written by the Spirit on human hearts, echoing Jeremiah's new covenant.
38157: A victorious general paraded through Rome with captives, incense burning along the route; some captives were led to execution. Paul pictures himself as a captive in God's triumphal procession, spreading the fragrance of Christ, a shocking image of apostleship as defeat that becomes victory.
38159: Greco-Roman rhetoric allowed self-praise only under strict conditions and found it distasteful. Paul knows boasting is foolish but turns the convention inside out by boasting of his weaknesses, a technique scholars call a 'fool's speech'.
38161: Cheap, fragile pottery lamps and storage jars were everywhere in Corinth, which had a large pottery industry. Treasure in clay jars means divine glory carried in breakable human bodies.
38163: In the ancient world gifts created reciprocal bonds. Paul presents the collection for Jerusalem as charis (grace) that flows from God's gift in Christ, aiming at 'equality' (isotēs) between churches, not patron-client dependency.
38165: Romans awarded a 'wall crown' to the first soldier over an enemy wall. Paul climaxes his list of credentials by being lowered down a wall in a basket to escape, a deliberate anti-boast.
38166:
The heart of 2 Corinthians is a Jewish argument about covenants. In chapter 3 Paul compares his ministry with Moses'. He does not call the Sinai covenant evil: it came with glory so bright that Moses had to veil his face (Exod 34:29-35). But the new covenant promised by Jeremiah and Ezekiel, with the Spirit writing on hearts of flesh rather than tablets of stone (Jer 31:31-34, Ezek 36:26-27), has a greater and lasting glory (2 Cor 3:6-11). When Paul says a veil lies over the reading of Moses for many of his fellow Jews, he adds that 'when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed' (2 Cor 3:16), quoting Moses' own action of going in to speak with God.

This passage has often been read in an anti-Jewish way, as if Judaism were a religion of death. Scholars in dialogue with Jewish readers, including contributors to the Jewish Annotated New Testament and 'Paul within Judaism' writers, stress that Paul speaks as an insider making an intra-Jewish claim about the age of the Spirit, much as the Qumran community claimed to be the people of the new covenant. Traditional Reformed readers (Scott Hafemann, for example) emphasise that Paul does see a real contrast between the letter that kills and the Spirit who gives life, rooted in Israel's hard-heartedness in the wilderness, not in any defect of the Law itself.

Other Jewish threads run through the letter: God's comfort in suffering (Isa 40:1, echoed in 2 Cor 1:3-7), the new creation of Isaiah (Isa 43:18-19, Isa 65:17) behind 'the old has gone, the new has come' (2 Cor 5:17), and the collection for Jerusalem, which Paul treats almost like the pilgrimage of the nations bringing gifts to Zion (Isa 60:5). Even his opponents' claim to be 'Hebrews, Israelites, Abraham's offspring' shows that the debate was between Jews about what faithfulness to Israel's God now looks like.
38167: Paul blesses the God of all comfort after near-death in Asia and explains why he changed his travel plans.

38212: In 2 Corinthians the pattern of Jesus' life becomes the pattern of ministry. 'Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor' (2 Cor 8:9); 'he was crucified in weakness but lives by the power of God' (2 Cor 13:4). Believers see God's glory 'in the face of Jesus Christ' (2 Cor 4:6), language that recalls Moses seeing God's glory on Sinai. 2 Corinthians 5:21, 'him who knew no sin he made to be sin for us', is a key text for substitutionary atonement in Reformed theology; N. T. Wright reads its second half ('that we might become the righteousness of God') as about apostles embodying God's covenant faithfulness, a view others (Moo, Gathercole) dispute. 38215: Paul is raising famine relief for poor Jewish believers in Jerusalem. The harvest he promises is that God will supply enough so the givers can keep being generous ('so that you may abound in every good work', 2 Cor 9:8), that righteousness will grow, and that many will thank God (2 Cor 9:10-13). He quotes Psalm 112 about the generous person who scatters gifts to the poor. The aim is 'equality' between churches (2 Cor 8:13-15), echoing the manna in Exodus 16, where no one had too much or too little.
38216: Evangelical scholars such as Murray Harris and David Garland agree with this reading and strongly reject prosperity-gospel uses. They add, fairly, that Paul does promise that God will provide for generous givers' needs and reward generosity, so giving is never pure loss; the point is that the 'return' is sufficiency for further giving, not personal wealth. This is a popular misreading; there is little scholarly disagreement.
38217: Read in context, the passage calls for cross-cultural generosity to the poor, not investment in one's own blessing.

38219: If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature: the old personal habits are gone and the believer is a brand new person.

The context is cosmic: God reconciling 'the world' (2 Cor 5:19), and a new way of knowing people 'not according to the flesh' (2 Cor 5:16). Believers belong to God's new creation already breaking into the old age.
38221: Evangelical scholars generally accept that both are present: the new world has begun in Christ, and the individual united to him really is changed. Hubbard argues the individual inner renewal is primary in this verse. The popular reading is not wrong, only too small.
38222: If new creation is cosmic as well as personal, salvation includes how believers see others, cross social boundaries and hope for the renewal of all things.
38223: The Corinthians were asked to stop judging leaders by charisma, credentials and eloquence and to recognise the crucified Messiah in a scarred, unimpressive apostle. They were also asked to keep their promise of giving to poor Jewish believers.
38224: In an age of celebrity pastors, platform-building and image management, 2 Corinthians is a corrective: true ministry is accountable, unpaid by patrons where needed, open about weakness and marked by suffering love. It also offers deep comfort to people in chronic pain or failure: 'my grace is sufficient for you' (2 Cor 12:9).
